newsitem.title: USA: HICKS, MUSE HAS CHOICES AFTER LIN -ANALYSTS.
newsitem.headline: HICKS, MUSE HAS CHOICES AFTER LIN -ANALYSTS.

text.p: Armed with its just-acquired LIN Television Corp stations, Hicks, Muse, Tate & Furst Inc will move aggresively into broadcasting, either acquiring more big-city stations or adding mid-market outlets.
Regardless of the route, there is little doubt among observers that the private firm is on an acquisition march.
"They're going to be opportunistic," said Vinton Vickers, an analyst at Furman Selz. "It's a consolidating TV market, and they're going to move in a bold, aggressive fashion."
Hicks, Muse officials were not immediately available for comment.
"Hicks Muse will be opportunistic," said Frank Bodenchak at Morgan Stanley. "They're looking at TV stations as a business" rather than plotting strategically by market size.
"With Hicks, Muse, you don't know which way they want to go," said Tim Wallace, an analyst at Lehman Brothers. "LIN offers an opportunity to go in two directions."
Wallace said the acquistion of KXAS-TV in Dallas gives them a beachhead into the big-city arena. The NBC affiliate, a big generator of cash flow, also gives them flexibility and leverage.
"They need a vehicle to get into the big markets, and the Dallas station is as good a horse to ride as any," said Dennis McAlpine at Josephthal Lyon & Ross.
But a move into big-city stations is tough. "It's difficult to buy big-market TV stations; they don't come on the block that often," Wallace said. "It's a slower process."

LIN holds a powerful block of mid-market stations, including KXAN in Austin, Texas; WANE in Fort Wayne, Indiana, and WAND in Decatur, Illinois. Those outlets fit well with Hicks, Muse's four mid-market stations, which are part of its Sunrise Television business. Purchases of three other stations are pending.
Hicks, Muse said, in a statement, it had no current plans to combine the activities of Sunrise and LIN.
Analysts said Hicks, Muse was drawn to LIN because of its high operating margins and respected management.
"LIN has some of the highest margins out there, 48 percent for the entire group," said Vickers.
Also, LIN chief executive Gary Chapman is viewed by analysts as having done a good job.
"Chapman has proven over and over that he has a strong sense of vision," especially as the industry moves from analog to digital technology, said Bodenchak.
Analysts lauded Chapman for pushing local marketing agreements (LMAs), in which the company pays a lease fee to operate a TV station, and keeps the revenues.
They said Chapman has stratetgically positioned LIN to benefit if digital technology brings about changes in U.S. rules that limit companies from owning more than one station in a city.
Analysts agreed that the price paid by Hicks, Muse was justified. The $47.50 cash per share for LIN was below the Tuesday closing price of 48-10/16.
Analysts explained the difference by saying that high expectations about a deal, which was long expected, drove arbitrageurs to push the stock too high.

AT&T Corp, which owns about 45 percent of LIN's outstanding shares, had an option to buy the company next year, or it could have put the broadcaster in play then, likely at a higher price, analyst said.
